one_sentence: Unforced convergence among independent AI systems constitutes a qualitatively stronger form of evidence than engineered multi-agent consensus.
executive_summary: This paper argues that when multiple AI systems from different providers independently analyze the same document and converge on the same structural conclusion without communication, that convergence is a form of evidence distinct from single-AI analysis or engineered multi-agent consensus. The author presents a proof-of-concept Constitutional Coherence Audit in which four AI systems (ChatGPT, Gemini P1, Perplexity, Gemini P2) were prompted separately and converged on aggregate scores of 1.0, 2.6, and 3.4 out of 10 on an author-intent standard, with the outlier (6.6) revealing a critical distinction between legal doctrine and original intent. The paper formalizes this as the Biaxiosum AI Evaluation System (BAES) and provides falsification criteria. The conclusion is that unforced convergence—agreement that emerges without being arranged—provides evidence that engineered consensus cannot, and that divergence is often more informative than agreement.
short_summary: This document is a methodology paper proposing the Biaxiosum AI Evaluation System (BAES) for evaluating AI agreement without engineered consensus. The core structural claim is that unforced convergence among independent AI systems constitutes evidence qualitatively different from single-AI analysis or multi-agent debate. The key evidence is a Constitutional Coherence Audit where four AI systems from different providers independently converged on similar scores (1.0–3.4/10) on an author-intent standard, with the outlier revealing a critical distinction. This matters because it offers a method to detect genuine signal in AI analysis, avoiding the circularity of engineered agreement and treating divergence as informative data.
